blocks.title: Nucleic acids
blocks.text: Nucleic acids are large biomolecules that store and transmit genetic information. They are polymers made up of smaller units called nucleotides.

Nucleic acids are formed from the nucleotide chains containing alternating sugar and phosphate groups with organic bases attached to the sugar molecules. The sugars are ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA; these are five-membered sugar molecules. Nucleotides joined together by a phosphodiester linkage with the '5' and '3' carbon atoms of the sugar to form nucleic acids (Figure 27.13). The process is repeated up to several million times to make a polynucleotide. Phosphodiester linkages are strong covalent bonds, which gives strength and stability to the polynucleotide chain.

blocks.alt: Left: two nucleotides. At the 5' end a phosphate is bonded to the 5' CH2 of a five-membered sugar ring carrying a BASE; the sugar's 3' carbon is bonded through O to a second phosphate, the phosphodiester linkage, which joins the 5' CH2 of the next sugar and base; that sugar ends in 3' OH, the 3' end of the chain. Right: the chain as alternating phosphate and sugar units with a base on each sugar.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.13: The general structure of nucleotide chains in nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.13; the linking phosphate is corrected).
blocks.long_description: In the phosphodiester linkage the oxygen from the 3' carbon is single-bonded to phosphorus, and the P=O double bond is to a non-bridging oxygen.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 27.13 draws the 3' oxygen double-bonded to phosphorus in the phosphodiester link; the 3' O–P bond is single and the P=O is on a non-bridging oxygen, as drawn above.
